If you need more than a kilowatt-hour on day one, the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max starts at 2,048Wh and goes to 6kWh. If you are backing up a house, the Anker SOLIX F3800 goes to 53.8kWh. 
 Expansion is the most under-weighted spec in this category, and the reason is that it only matters in hindsight. Nobody regrets it on the day they buy. They regret it eighteen months later, when the van build grew, or the outage lasted two days instead of one, and the only route forward is to buy a second whole unit — inverter, screen, ports and all — because the first one was sealed shut.

The Gen 2 case is the sharper one — Anker's newer unit dropped the expansion its predecessor had, which is the central trade in that comparison . The BLUETTI AC180 does not expand either. 
 What to look for before you pay for expandability
 Does the inverter grow too? No. This is the thing people get wrong. An expansion battery adds watt-hours, not watts. A 1,800W unit with 5kWh behind it is still an 1,800W unit — it will run your fridge for three days instead of one, and it still will not start an RV air conditioner. If your problem is output rather than runtime, expansion is the wrong purchase and what size power station do I need explains the difference between the two numbers. 
 Can you refill the stack? A 5kWh battery and a 400W solar ceiling is a mismatch — you would need days of sun to fill it once. This is why the EcoFlow units dominate this page: 1,000W of input on the 1kWh and 2kWh models, 2,400W on the Anker F3800. How much solar input do you need does the arithmetic properly. 
 Is the expansion battery still sold? An expansion ecosystem is only as good as its availability three years out. This is a genuine risk and not one we can resolve from a spec sheet — but it is a reason to prefer a current, high-volume platform over a discontinued one, and a reason to buy the pack sooner rather than later if you are confident you will want it. 
 Does it add weight you will then have to move? An expansion pack for a 1kWh unit typically weighs about as much as the unit. Two 28 lb boxes are not a 56 lb box; they are two trips. For a van or a basement that is fine. For a tent pitch it is the end of the idea.

 If your requirement is already clear and stable — one night of CPAP, a weekend fridge, a router through an evening — then buying an expandable platform costs you weight and output for an option you will never exercise.  Can I Add Another Battery to My Solar System Later?
 ✎ Written by Peter Yin ✓ Reviewed by: Technical Review Team ◷ September 6, 2026 10 min read 
 Share: 
 “Yes, this battery is expandable.”
 That sentence appears in many quotations. It sounds reassuring, but it leaves out the part that matters three years later: expandable with which model, at what age, under which firmware, and with whose written approval?
 Adding storage after the first installation is often possible. It is not automatic. A new battery can have the same brand name and the same nominal voltage as the old one and still be a poor match for the existing system.
 Quick answer: You may be able to add another battery later, but you need to check the exact battery model, voltage platform, usable capacity, BMS protocol, firmware, state of health, inverter limits, approved parallel quantity and warranty terms before ordering the new module.
 Battery health and inverter compatibility review 
 “Expandable” can mean four different things
 Suppliers use the word expandable for several system designs. Ask which one the quotation actually describes.
 Expansion route 
 What changes 
 What can stop the project 
 Add the same battery model in parallel 
 Battery kWh and available current may increase 
 Model, BMS, age, cable, protection or inverter limits 
 Add approved modules to a stack 
 The system grows within a defined product family 
 Stack height, module generation, firmware and controller limits 
 Add a separate AC-coupled battery system 
 A second battery and inverter system is installed 
 Space, energy management, transfer logic and local rules 
 Replace the original battery with a larger bank 
 The old battery is removed and the system is rebuilt 
 Cost, disposal, inverter compatibility and warranty reset 
 These routes do not deliver the same result. Adding battery capacity increases stored energy. It does not automatically increase the inverter's AC output power. If the inverter can deliver 5kW, connecting more batteries does not turn it into a 10kW inverter.
 A real product example: expansion numbers are not a lifetime promise
 CVC's Firefly Low Voltage product material describes a 51.2Vdc LiFePO4 family with 3.6kWh, 7.2kWh, 10.8kWh and 14.4kWh configurations. It lists CAN, RS485 and WiFi communication, and states that expansion can reach up to three systems and 43.2kWh, subject to system design.
 That is useful information for a new quotation. It tells an installer that the platform has a defined expansion path today. It does not guarantee that an identical module will still be available three years from now, or that a new module can be mixed with an older one without a health and firmware review.
 The same point appears in the Firefly Max material . The product data lists 16.179kWh nominal capacity, 14.561kWh usable capacity and up to 15 units in parallel, subject to system design. Those are current product and system limits. They should not be rewritten as a promise of future spare-part availability.
 The broader energy storage battery portfolio is useful for comparing platforms, but expansion still depends on the exact model, system limits and written approval.
 Battery expansion compatibility review for an old battery, new battery, inverter and BMS 
 The numbers that must match before you add a battery
 “Both batteries are 51.2V” is not enough.
 For example, CVC's IPL-51314H is specified as a 51.2V, 314Ah, 16kWh LiFePO4 battery. Its published operating voltage range is 43.2V to 57.6V, with CAN2.0 and RS485 communication, a maximum continuous charge and discharge current of 157A, and up to 32 parallel units. Those figures describe that model. They do not make it an automatic expansion partner for every other 51.2V battery.
 The nominal energy calculation is simple:
 51.2V × 314Ah ÷ 1,000 ≈ 16.08kWh 
 The integration decision is not simple. Before placing the new order, compare the original battery and the proposed battery using the fields below.
 Check 
 What to compare 
 Why it matters 
 Model 
 Full model number and product generation 
 Brand-level matching is too broad 
 Chemistry 
 LiFePO4 cell chemistry and approved configuration 
 Different cell behaviour changes the charge and discharge response 
 Voltage 
 Nominal voltage and operating range 
 A similar label may hide different cut-off limits 
 Capacity 
 Ah, nominal kWh and usable kWh 
 The BMS and inverter may calculate SOC differently 
 Current 
 Continuous and peak charge/discharge limits 
 The parallel bank must share current within approved limits 
 Communication 
 CAN, RS485, protocol profile and register map 
 A connector that fits does not prove usable communication 
 Firmware 
 Battery, master BMS and inverter versions 
 New firmware may change alarms, SOC logic or addressing 
 Health 
 SOH, internal resistance, cell balance and cycle history 
 A three-year-old battery may not behave like a new module 
 Physical installation 
 Rack, stack, cable length, breaker, ventilation and access 
 Unequal resistance and poor service access create system problems 
 Warranty 
 Written approval for the exact mixed configuration 
 Verbal compatibility does not settle warranty responsibility 
 Why a three-year gap changes the answer
 The battery did not remain frozen while it sat on the wall. It accumulated charge and discharge cycles, calendar age, firmware updates and service history. The inverter may also have changed its software or communication profile.
 Three years later, check these questions before comparing prices:
 Is the original model still produced?
 If the model has been discontinued, ask for the official replacement model and a written compatibility statement. “Same voltage” is not a replacement policy.
 Is the original firmware still supported?
 The new module may ship with a different firmware version. Confirm whether the modules can use one approved version, whether a firmware update is required and who performs it.
 How healthy is the installed battery?
 Request a BMS report that includes SOH, cell voltage spread, temperature history and fault history. The exact acceptance limits should come from the manufacturer or system integrator. Do not invent a universal SOH threshold and apply it to every battery family.
 What does the inverter allow?
 The inverter may limit the maximum battery current, number of battery units, usable voltage range or supported protocol. If the system is already close to its current limit, adding capacity may increase runtime without increasing the output power available to the loads.
 Does the warranty cover the new configuration?
 The answer should be written into the quotation or technical agreement. It should identify the original battery, the new battery, the inverter, the approved wiring or controller and the party responsible for commissioning.
 Commercial rule: “Expandable” describes a design intention. A three-year expansion requires a model-specific compatibility decision and a new commissioning record.
 Battery expansion planning illustration 3 
 Supplier answers that are not enough
 When a supplier replies quickly, compare the sentence with the evidence it should produce.
 Supplier answer 
 What you should request instead 
 “Our battery supports expansion.” 
 Maximum quantity, approved topology and exact model list 
 “The new battery is the same brand.” 
 Full model, generation, voltage range and BMS compatibility 
 “It is also 51.2V.” 
 Operating voltage, current limits, SOC logic and communication profile 
 “The inverter is compatible.” 
 Inverter model, firmware, protocol and approved battery configuration 
 “You can add more later.” 
 Product lifecycle plan, replacement model and spare-module availability 
 “The warranty will be fine.” 
 Written warranty treatment for the mixed or expanded system 
 “The installer can configure it on site.” 
 Installation procedure, addressing method, balance requirements and acceptance test 
 This is where many expansion projects become expensive. The battery price is visible. The missing documentation, return shipment, site visit and warranty argument arrive later.
 A practical three-year expansion review
 Use this sequence before requesting a final price.
 Collect the original quotation, datasheet, manual, serial number, installation date and commissioning record.
 Record the inverter brand, model, firmware, battery protocol and current battery quantity.
 Read the existing BMS data and save the SOH, SOC, cell voltage spread and fault history.
 Compare the original and proposed batteries line by line, including model generation and communication settings.
 Confirm the inverter's maximum battery current, voltage range and approved parallel quantity.
 Ask the supplier to state whether the new module can be mixed with the existing module and under what conditions.
 Get the warranty position in writing before payment.
 After installation, test battery recognition, SOC synchronisation, charge current, discharge current, alarms, monitoring and backup output.
 The commissioning report should identify which battery is old, which module is new, the firmware versions used, the test conditions and the person who approved the final configuration.
 The better way to specify an expandable battery at the first order
 If future expansion matters, do not ask only for today's capacity. Add future supply to the original specification:
 initial model and capacity
 expansion model or approved replacement model
 maximum expansion quantity
 expected product lifecycle and last-order notice
 firmware control and update responsibility
 minimum documentation kept for each battery batch
 procedure for mixing new and existing modules
 warranty treatment after expansion
 spare parts and after-sales response
 This turns “expandable” into something that can be quoted, tested and supported.
 CVC's home battery supplier checklist for installers and battery-inverter compatibility article cover related checks. For a project that includes a new battery family, send the installed model, inverter model, installation date, target capacity and destination market through the contact page .
 Common questions
 Can I add another battery to my solar system after three years?
 You can add another battery after three years only when the exact model, battery health, firmware, inverter limits, communication protocol and the manufacturer's written approval all support the expansion. The installation date alone does not decide compatibility.
 Can I mix a new battery with an old battery of the same brand?
 Do not assume so. The model, generation, voltage range, BMS, SOH and firmware all need to be checked. Some manufacturers approve the combination. Others require the modules to match more closely or require a full battery-bank replacement.
 Does adding more batteries increase inverter power?
 No. It usually increases stored energy and may improve available DC current, but the inverter's rated AC output remains the inverter's rated AC output.
 Is a higher nominal kWh always better for expansion?
 No. Usable capacity, current capability, inverter compatibility, installation space and future module supply matter just as much as nominal kWh. CVC's guide on comparing energy storage batteries beyond nominal capacity explains this broader check.
 The buying rule
 If you may need more storage later, treat expansion as part of the first purchase. Ask for the future model, future firmware path, future warranty treatment and future supply plan before you approve the first battery.
 The useful question is not “Can this battery be expanded?” It is “Can this exact system still be expanded, supported and documented three years from now?”
 For a product and compatibility review, send the original battery datasheet, inverter model, installation date and desired capacity to the CVC contact team .

 Sometimes—but only when the exact power station model supports a manufacturer-approved expansion battery. Before buying, check the station’s full model name and generation, its compatibility list and manual, the permitted number of batteries, and the required connection method. A matching battery can add stored energy and extend runtime; it does not automatically increase the station’s output wattage.
 What to check before buying an expansion battery 
 Identify the exact station. Record the full model name and version, not just the brand or product family. Expansion support can differ between models in the same range.
 Find the approved battery. Check the manufacturer’s compatibility list and the station’s manual. Match the battery to the specific station; a similar-looking connector does not prove compatibility. Jackery, for example, lists supported models and says its expansion batteries are model-specific and not compatible with other station models ( Jackery Support, August 6, 2026 ).
 Check the expansion limit and connection requirements. Confirm how many packs the station allows and whether the exact setup requires a particular cable, hub, adapter, or firmware. Follow the manual for that model rather than assuming instructions carry over from another station.
 Compare capacity and output separately. Capacity, measured in watt-hours (Wh), describes stored energy. Added capacity can extend runtime, depending on the load and conversion losses. Output wattage is a separate rating that determines which appliances the station can run; adding a battery does not, by itself, establish that output wattage rises.
 Read the safe-handling instructions. Check when to power down, connect, charge, disconnect, and store the system. Do not improvise a connection or remove a battery while the system is operating if the manual prohibits it.

Which Jackery Expansion Battery Fits Which Station? 
 Skip to content

 · ★ 4.7 from 14,397 product reviews 
 The short version: Three expansion batteries, and each fits a short list. Battery Pack 2000 Plus v2 fits the HomePower 2000 Plus v2 and 1000 Plus v2. Battery Pack 3600 fits the HomePower 3600 Plus and 3600 Pro Max. Battery Pack 5000 Plus fits the Explorer 5000 Plus and nothing else. Several popular stations, including the Explorer 1000 v2, 1500 v2, 1500 Ultra, 2000 v2 and HomePower 1000 v2, take no expansion battery at all .
 Why this is the decision you cannot undo
 You can add solar later. You can add a transfer switch later. You cannot add expandability later. If you buy a station that does not accept packs and then find you need more capacity, the only move is buying a second complete station.
 Sizing it for your own rig? Skip the wattage tables and size your own off-grid system in about a minute.
 So if there is any chance your needs will grow, pay attention to this list before you pick the base unit, not after.
 Battery Pack 2000 Plus v2
 2,048Wh of LiFePO4 rated at 6,000 cycles to 70% or better capacity. It fits the HomePower 2000 Plus v2 and the HomePower 1000 Plus v2 .
 Each station accepts up to five packs. On the 2000 Plus v2 that takes you to 12kWh. On the 1000 Plus v2, Jackery quotes up to 11kWh. The pack charges through the station from a wall outlet or solar, has its own LCD for battery percentage and fault codes, and shuts the display off after two hours idle.
 This is the cheapest route into a system that grows: start with the HomePower 1000 Plus v2 and add packs as the budget allows.
 Battery Pack 3600
 3,584Wh, over 6,000 cycles, fitting the HomePower 3600 Plus and the HomePower 3600 Pro Max .
 One station takes five packs for 21.5kWh. Two stations in parallel take ten packs for 43kWh. It has dual handles because it is a two-person lift into a storage bay, and it operates down to -20 C, which matters for winter use.
 The useful detail: because it fits both 3600-series stations, the packs carry over if you change base units later.
 Battery Pack 5000 Plus
 5,040Wh, over 4,000 cycles, and it works with the Explorer 5000 Plus only . It meets UL1973 with a BMS managing charge and discharge, operates down to -15 C, and the dual-handle design is rated to carry over four times its own weight. It weighs about 81.6 lb.
 Stacking packs takes a 5000 Plus system toward 60kWh, which is house-scale rather than camper-scale.
 The stations that take no packs
 Worth stating plainly, because the product names do not warn you:
 Explorer 300D and Explorer 500 v2 
 Explorer 1000 v2 — the best seller, and not expandable
 HomePower 1000 v2 — note this is different from the 1000 Plus v2, which is expandable
 Explorer 1500 v2 and Explorer 1500 Ultra 
 Explorer 2000 v2 — again, different from the HomePower 2000 Plus v2
 HomePower 3000 — Jackery does not list an expansion battery for it
 The pattern, roughly: the word Plus in a HomePower name signals an expandable unit. It is not a perfect rule, but it is a good first filter.
 How much capacity do you actually need?
 Before buying packs, do the arithmetic. A 12V compressor fridge in a camper runs somewhere around 400 to 600Wh a day. Lights, a water pump, phone and laptop charging add maybe 200 to 300Wh. So a typical trailer without air conditioning or heating is doing 600 to 900Wh a day.
 Against that, a 2,048Wh station is two days of margin, and a 3,584Wh unit is three or more. Most people who think they need expansion actually need solar, because the problem is not storage but refilling it. The SolarSaga 500 X or the DC-DC alternator charger often solves it for less money than a pack.
 FAQ
 Can I use a Battery Pack 3600 on a HomePower 3000?
 No. Jackery lists the Battery Pack 3600 for the HomePower 3600 Plus and 3600 Pro Max. The 3000 is a different unit.
 Does an expansion battery charge on its own?
 No. The packs charge through the connected station, from a wall outlet or from solar. They are not standalone batteries.
 Will adding packs make the inverter more powerful?
 No, and this is a common misunderstanding. Packs add capacity, which is runtime. The station's output rating in watts does not change, so what you can run at once stays the same.
 Can I mix pack models?
 No. Each pack is specified for its own station family, and they are not interchangeable across families.

 FAQ
How do I recharge the DBS1000 Pro? 
 For single DBS1000 Pro unit, you can charge it with AC (1200W), solar panels (1200W Max), AC + solar panels(1200W Max) and car charger (126W).
How many solar panels can I use to charge DBS1000 Pro? 
 DBS1000 Pro can be charged with solar panels that have MC4 connector at maximum 1200W and the combined voltage and current of the solar panels must be within 12-60 volts and under 25 amps.
In additional, DBS2000B expandable battery also has standalone solar charging capability with maximum 1200W input. The combined voltage and current of the solar panels must be between 12-60 volts and under 25 amps.
Can I use other brands of solar panel to charge? 
 Yes, you can use most solar panels with MC4 connectors. Dabbsson uses a standard XT60 port for solar recharging. Ensure you use a sturdy MC4 to XT60 cable or use the solar charging cable that come with Dabbsson power station and make sure that the solar panels meet the specific requirements of the Dabbsson power station.
How does DBS1000 Pro expandable output work? 
 DBS1000 Pro can increase the output to 2400W by simply adding one expandable battery DBS2000B/DBS2100B. 
Connect two DBS1000 Pro using the parallel connector for 3800W output. 
Connect two DBS1000 Pro and two DBS2000B/DBS2100B for maximum 4600W output.
How to connect the DBS1000 Pro to Dabbsson App? 
 First you'll need to download Dabbsson App from the app store or Dabbsson official website. Then connect your phone to home Wi-Fi and turn on the bluetooth. After that, you can choose to search the nearby Dabbsson devices or add DBS1000 Pro manually according to the steps.
How do I update the firmware? 
 First, connect DBS1000 Pro to the app and ensure the network is working. Then, go to the firmware section in the power station settings within the app to check for updates and follow the steps to complete the process.
What is the DBS1000 Pro battery cycle life? 
 Using Semi-Solid LiFePO4 batteries, DBS1000 Pro has a 4000 + 500 (extra cycles with BMS) before the capacity drop to 80%+. (Tested in lab under 25℃ environment)
How to store and maintain DBS1000 Pro portable power station? 
 1. To make the most use of the battery life, we recommend using the portable power station in an environment of 20℃ to 30℃ and keep it away from water and heating source .
2. For long-term storage, discharge the battery to 30% and recharge it to 60% every three months.
3. For safety reasons, Dabbsson power station should be store in a dry environment and the temperature should be between 45℃ and -10℃.
How to use Dabbsson EPS function? 
 When a power outage occurs, Dabbsson EPS automatically switches to battery power within 15ms to keep your appliance running. 
Simply connect the Dabbsson power station to a wall outlet, then plug in the appliance you want to protect. Enable standby mode and set the power station's AC timeout to 'Never' in the Dabbsson App to ensure it's always on.
In this setup, the power station operates in pass-through mode, allowing grid power to flow through to the appliance. If the grid power fails, it seamlessly switches to battery power within 15ms to keep your protected appliances always on.
Can I use EPS mode all the time？ 
 Yes, you can.
For battery lifespan consideration, discharge the power station normally to 30% and charge it back up in every 30 days.
How to achieve 10240Wh expandable capacity? 
 Connect two DBS1000 Pro (1024Wh each) using the Dabbsson parallel connector and add four DBS2000B expandable batteries (2048Wh each) to get maximum 10240Wh capacity.
How to add an expandable battery to the power station？ 
 1. Connect the expandable battery cable while both the main unit and expandable battery are turned off. Insert the cable into the main unit first, followed by the battery.
2. If the expandable battery cable is connected while both the main unit and battery are powered on, a restart will be required.
